title: Sirach
subtitle: a Jerusalem teacher's book of wisdom, signed with his name, carried to Egypt by his grandson, its Hebrew lost for centuries until 1896
lead: Sirach is a book of wisdom from ancient Israel, and a long one: fifty-one chapters after its prologue. Its author signs it: "I, Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem" (50:27), a teacher and scribe known in Hebrew as Ben Sira. He wrote in Hebrew in Jerusalem about 180 BC, and his grandson, who arrived in Egypt "in the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes" (132 BC), translated the book into Greek and wrote the prologue that opens it.

Most of the book is teaching in the style of Proverbs, addressed to "my child": the fear of the Lord, honor for parents, humility, speech, friendship, money, lending, women and marriage, children and servants, health and the doctor, banquets, death. Into this Ben Sira sets hymns and prayers, Wisdom's own speech, in which she pitches her tent in Israel and turns out to be "the book of the covenant of God Most High, the law Moses commanded" (24:23), and a long "Hymn of the Fathers" (44–50) that praises Israel's heroes from Enoch to Nehemiah and ends with Simon the high priest of Ben Sira's own day.

Catholic and Orthodox Christians read Sirach in their Old Testament, and the early Latin church read it so often in public that it was called Ecclesiasticus, the church book. Anglicans and Lutherans place it among the Apocrypha, and other Protestants do not count it as Scripture. It is not in the Jewish Bible, though the rabbis quoted it. Its Hebrew was lost for centuries until 1896, when leaves of it turned up from the storeroom of a Cairo synagogue; a Hebrew scroll with much of chapters 39–44, copied in the first century BC, later came to light at Masada. This site translates the grandson's Greek, in the order of the Greek manuscripts: in chapters 30–36 that order differs from the KJV and most English Bibles (see "The order of chapters 30–36").
facts: Scripture for

The Catholic Church (Trent, 1546), the Eastern Orthodox churches (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672) and the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, whose Old Testament list names the "Book of Joshua the son of Sirac."
Not Scripture for

Anglicans (Article VI names "Jesus the Son of Sirach" among the books the church reads "for example of life") and Lutherans, who place it among the Apocrypha; Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches; and Judaism.
Author

Jesus (Hebrew Yeshua) son of Eleazar son of Sirach, of Jerusalem (50:27), a scribe and teacher; in Hebrew, Ben Sira. Manuscript B of the Hebrew, at 50:27 and 51:30, calls him "Simeon son of Yeshua son of Eleazar ben Sira" (Rendsburg and Binstein). Toy and Lévi note that he alone of the Old Testament and apocryphal writers signed his work.
Translator
His grandson, who does not give his name. He came to Egypt in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes, stayed there, and translated the book for Jews living abroad (the prologue).
Date

Written about 180 BC (Rendsburg and Binstein; Gigot gives between 190 and 170 BC); translated in Egypt after 132 BC. The grandson arrived "in the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes"; the second Ptolemy called Euergetes (Ptolemy VIII) shared the throne from 170 BC and counted his years from then, so that year is 132 BC (Gigot). The date also rests on taking the high priest of 50:1, "Simon son of Onias" (Toy and Lévi note that the Hebrew calls him son of Johanan), as Simon II, high priest from 226 to 199 BC in Toy and Lévi's dates; those who took him for Simon I put the book about a century earlier (Gigot). The book shows no sign of the persecution under Antiochus, which Toy and Lévi date to 168 BC.
Setting

Jerusalem in the time of the high priest Simon (50:1–21): a temple city ruled by its high priests, with scribes who studied the law and served among the powerful (38:24–39:11). In Simon's day, Gigot notes from Josephus, Judea was harassed by hostile armies and invaded by Antiochus. The grandson's Greek was made for Jews in Egypt.
Original language

Hebrew. About two-thirds of the Hebrew survives (Rendsburg and Binstein; the NETS introduction): leaves of six medieval manuscripts from the Cairo Genizah, called A to F, found from 1896 on; a scroll from Masada with much of 39:27–44:17, copied in the first century BC; and two pieces from Qumran, 2Q18 with fragments of 6:14–15 and 6:20–31, and the Psalms Scroll 11QPs-a with 51:13–20 and 51:30 (column 21, lines 11–17, and column 22, line 1).
Surviving in

Greek (Codex Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, 300s–400s AD; some later Greek copies add lines, the "longer text"); Syriac, made from the Hebrew; Latin, an Old Latin version that Jerome left almost unrevised, with many additions; and the Hebrew above.
Kind of writing

Wisdom teaching in two-line verses, like Proverbs, with hymns of praise (39:12–35; 42:15–43:33), prayers (22:27–23:6; 33:1–13 with 36:16–22; 51:1–12), Wisdom's speech (24), a survey of Israel's history in praise of its great men (44–50) and a closing poem on the search for wisdom (51:13–30).
Numbering on this site

The Greek order and numbers of Swete's edition, which keeps the order of the Greek manuscripts. In 30:25–36:16 two long blocks stand in the reverse order from the KJV, the Latin and the Hebrew; Ziegler's Göttingen edition, which NETS and the NRSV follow, restores the Hebrew and Latin order (NETS introduction). Other Bibles and editions may number these chapters differently, so check before citing; the table under "The order of chapters 30–36" matches every verse with the KJV.
Length
The grandson's prologue and 51 chapters, 1,402 verse numbers; 34 of those numbers have no line in Codex Vaticanus and belong to the longer Greek text, shown in brackets.
authorship: Near the end the author names himself: "I, Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem, who rained down wisdom from his heart" (50:27; the Greek has "Sirach Eleazar" side by side). Manuscript B of the Hebrew, at 50:27 and 51:30, reads "Simeon son of Yeshua son of Eleazar ben Sira" (Rendsburg and Binstein). The Jewish Encyclopedia (Toy and Lévi) judged that the evidence points to "Jesus, son of Simon, son of Eleazar ben Sira," and noted that he alone of the Old Testament and apocryphal writers signed his work. Sirach (Greek Seirach) is the Hebrew Sira, a family name.

The translator calls Ben Sira "my grandfather Jesus" and says he gave himself to reading "the law, the prophets and the other books of our ancestors" until he was led to write something of his own on instruction and wisdom. The grandson came to Egypt, found there people who wanted to learn, and spent long nights making the translation. He apologizes that "Words spoken in Hebrew do not carry the same force when they are carried over into another language," and says the same is true of the law, the prophecies and the rest of the books.

The early church knew the author's name: Jerome speaks of "the book of the model of virtue (panaretos) Jesus son of Sirach," and Rufinus of "the Wisdom of the Son of Syrach." Because its style resembles Proverbs, some counted it among the books of Solomon: Cyprian quotes it "in Solomon, in Ecclesiasticus," and the Council of Carthage (397) counted "five books of Solomon." Augustine explained that it had been customary to ascribe Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus to Solomon, but that "the more learned have no doubt that they are not his" (City of God 17.20).

Luther's preface says the book's right name is "Jesus Syrach." He thought that the grandson, finishing in Egypt the book his grandfather had begun, "gathered the best from many books" (our translation of "aus vielen Büchern zusamen gelesen das beste"), so that it is not set in order one piece after another. The Catholic and Jewish encyclopedias of the early 1900s (Gigot; Toy and Lévi) accept the signature: one teacher wrote the book, whatever older sayings he took up, and his grandson translated it. The poem of 51:13–30 also circulated on its own: 51:13–20 and 51:30 stand among the psalms of the Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11QPs-a).

audience.to: Young men of Jerusalem's educated class, the sons of families who would become scribes, counselors, judges and officials, about 180 BC, studying with a teacher who calls them "my child" and invites them to lodge in his "house of instruction" (51:23; in the Hebrew, his beit midrash, "house of study"). They lived in a temple city under a high priest, in years when, Gigot notes from Josephus, Judea was harassed by hostile armies and invaded by Antiochus. A second audience came two generations later: the Greek-speaking Jews of Egypt, for whom the grandson translated the book after 132 BC so that they too could live "by the law" (the prologue).
audience.why: To train them to be wise in the way Israel understood wisdom: the fear of the Lord and the keeping of the law, shown in daily life at home, at table, in business, in court and before the powerful. Ben Sira claims that all wisdom comes from the Lord and lives in Israel's law (1:1; 24:23); against the temptation to blame God for sin he insists on human choice (15:11–20); and in the Hymn of the Fathers he gives his students a history to belong to, from Enoch to the high priest Simon whom they could see in the temple (44–50). Knowing this audience explains the book's mix of piety and practical advice, its interest in table manners and money, its warnings about women and daughters written by a man to young men in a patriarchal household, and its honor for priests and the temple.
views: Read at its word, 51:23 means that Ben Sira kept a school and the book gathers his lessons. His Hebrew "house of study" (beit midrash) is the name later used for the rabbis' houses of learning.
A book for a wider public

The grandson's prologue speaks of "those who love learning," both those who can read the books and "those outside," and his Greek was made for a whole community in Egypt. On this view the book was meant from the start for anyone who would read it, not only a circle of pupils.
Written with the high priesthood in view

In the Hebrew of 50:24, as Gigot translates it, Ben Sira prays for Simon, "may He establish with him the covenant of Phineas, that will endure with him and with his seed"; the grandson's Greek instead prays, "May he entrust his mercy to us, and may he set us free in his time" (50:24). Gigot (1909) took the Hebrew prayer as written while Simon was still alive, and the Greek as made when Simon had been dead for some time.

lenses.name: Catholic
lenses.desc: The Catholic Church counts Sirach, which it long called Ecclesiasticus, among the deuterocanonical books of the Old Testament: the Council of Trent (1546) named "Ecclesiasticus" among the sacred and canonical books, and the Catechism (120) lists "Sirach (Ecclesiasticus)." It is read at Mass on the feast of the Holy Family, on the Second Sunday after Christmas (Wisdom's praise in chapter 24) and on several Sundays of the year.

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The Orthodox churches read Sirach in the Greek Old Testament. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672) named "the Wisdom of Sirach" among the genuine parts of Scripture; other Orthodox teachers, following Athanasius, place it among the books "appointed to be read," as Philaret's catechism does (questions 34–35).

lenses.name: Protestant
lenses.desc: Protestants place Sirach among the Apocrypha. Luther called it a useful book for ordinary people and a book of household discipline, but said the old fathers did not count it as Holy Scripture. Anglicans read "Jesus the Son of Sirach" for example of life but not for doctrine (Article VI); Reformed and Baptist confessions give it no authority.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Scholars read Sirach as the signed work of a Jerusalem scribe and teacher, written in Hebrew about 180 BC, before the persecution under Antiochus, and translated into Greek by his grandson in Egypt after 132 BC. They use the Hebrew manuscripts found since 1896 to recover what Ben Sira wrote, and the book itself as a dated witness to Judaism between the Hebrew Bible and the Maccabees.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: Sirach is not in the Jewish Bible, and the Tosefta says the books of Ben Sira "do not defile the hands," that is, are not Scripture. Yet the rabbis quoted it by name, once even as "written in the Writings," a Hebrew copy made in the first century BC was found at Masada, and Jews were still copying it in the Middle Ages, as the leaves found in a Cairo synagogue show.

sections.b:
Read it the way it was written: as a teacher's lessons, gathered into a book. There is an order of a kind, with poems on wisdom and the fear of the Lord standing at the head of sections (1; 4:11–19; 14:20–15:10; 24; 38:24–39:11) and a long hymn at the end (42:15–50:24), but most chapters move from one subject to the next as a lesson would. Luther already noticed that the pieces are not set "in order one after another."

Hear who is speaking. Most of the book is the teacher speaking to "my child." Wisdom speaks in her own voice in chapter 24. Ben Sira prays in 22:27–23:6, 33:1–13 with 36:16–22, and 51:1–12, and speaks of himself in 24:30–34, 36:16 with 30:25–27 (KJV 33:16–18), 39:12 and 50:27–29. The grandson speaks only in the prologue.

Read it beside the books it knows. Ben Sira had studied "the law, the prophets and the other books of our ancestors" (the prologue), and it shows: Proverbs above all, but also Genesis, Deuteronomy, the Psalms, Job, and in chapters 44–49 the whole story from Genesis to Nehemiah. Where he takes up a verse of the 66 books, the notes quote it.

Watch the numbers. This site follows the Greek manuscripts. In chapters 30–36 the KJV, the Latin Vulgate, the Hebrew and most English Bibles have two long blocks the other way round, so the same verse can carry different numbers in different Bibles. The table below matches them.

The prologue is the only part of the book written first in Greek, and it gives the book a firm date. The grandson writes that he arrived in Egypt "in the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes" and lived there a while. Two Ptolemies had the title Euergetes ("Benefactor"). The first, Ptolemy III, reigned only twenty-five years. The second, Ptolemy VIII, shared the throne with his brother from 170 BC, and later ruled alone, but counted his years from 170, so his thirty-eighth year is 132 BC. The Catholic Encyclopedia (Gigot, 1909) and the Jewish Encyclopedia (Toy and Lévi) both reckon it so. Rendsburg and Binstein put the grandfather's book about 180 BC; Gigot, counting forty to sixty years back, between 190 and 170 BC; Toy and Lévi "in the first third of the second century." He praises the high priest Simon (50:1–21) and shows no sign of the persecution under Antiochus.

Three times the grandson names the books his grandfather studied: "the law and the prophets and the others who came after them," "the law, the prophets and the other books of our ancestors," and "the law itself, the prophecies and the rest of the books." So by 132 BC the grandson can speak of a Scripture in three parts, like the Jewish Bible's Torah, Prophets and Writings, and like Jesus' words "in the Law of Moses, in the Prophets and in the Psalms" (Luke 24:44). Readers differ on how much it shows: it may point to a third collection already closed, or, since the grandson never names the third group's books or gives it a title, "the others" may still have been an open shelf.

The grandson's apology is still the honest translator's creed: "Words spoken in Hebrew do not carry the same force when they are carried over into another language," and the same is true, he says, of the law, the prophecies and the other books in Greek. His words imply that these books were already read in another language, and that they differed there from the Hebrew. This site's Plain translates his Greek; the variant notes give the Hebrew where it differs.

From its first centuries the church read Sirach in translation: Greek, Latin, Syriac and others. Jerome speaks of a Hebrew copy in his day, titled "Parables" (in Hebrew Mishle), and rabbis quoted Hebrew lines from it, but Gigot notes that after the time of Saadia, in the 900s, "all documentary traces of a Hebrew text of Ecclesiasticus practically disappear from the Christian world." In 1896 the twin sisters Agnes Smith Lewis and Margaret Dunlop Gibson brought back to Cambridge Hebrew documents obtained in Cairo. Solomon Schechter recognized one leaf as the Hebrew of Sirach, from chapters 39 and 40, and published it in July 1896. A. E. Cowley and Adolf Neubauer then found nine more leaves of the same manuscript among fragments from the Genizah of a Cairo synagogue that had reached the Bodleian Library at Oxford, and published them in 1897. In the end leaves of six medieval manuscripts were identified, now called A to F, some as recently as 2007 and 2010 (Rendsburg and Binstein). Gigot (1909) dated the leaves known to him to the 900s or 1000s AD at the earliest.

Were these medieval leaves faithful to what Ben Sira wrote? Much older finds help to answer. Among the scrolls from Qumran, a small piece from Cave 2 (2Q18) holds fragments of 6:14–15 and 6:20–31, and the great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11 (11QPs-a) holds 51:13–20 and 51:30. Yigael Yadin's excavations at Masada found a Hebrew scroll with much of 39:27–44:17, which Yadin published in 1965; it was copied in the first century BC (Corley; the NETS introduction). Rendsburg and Binstein date the Qumran and Masada copies from about 50 BC to AD 70, "only a century or two after the work's original composition," and the Masada scroll and the Psalms Scroll overlap with the Genizah's manuscript B, so they can be compared line by line. The NETS translator, Benjamin Wright, judges that the Hebrew manuscripts "seem, in their essentials, to preserve the Hebrew of Ben Sira but not without numerous mistakes, additions and corruptions." About two-thirds of Ben Sira's Hebrew is now known.

The Hebrew does not replace the Greek on this site, because the Greek is the book the churches received and the Hebrew survives only in part. But it is Ben Sira's own language, and the variant notes give it wherever it differs in meaning. They cite it from the manuscripts themselves (A to F, Masada, 2Q18, 11QPs-a), naming the manuscript and its leaf or column, as Martin Abegg, Eric Reymond and others transcribe them in Rendsburg and Binstein's online edition; where David Kahana's edition (1912) is used instead, the note names it.

sections.h: The Greek, the Syriac and the Latin
sections.b:
The Greek. The grandson's translation survives in the great codices Vaticanus, Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus (300s–400s AD) and in many later copies. This site follows Swete's printed text, which is Codex Vaticanus, with the other codices in his notes. Some later Greek copies, and the Latin, have extra lines, a "longer text" (the NETS introduction calls it a later Greek recension). Among those copies the manuscript numbered 248 is, in the NETS translator's words, "one of the most important manuscript witnesses" for the added lines, though it "does not contain all" of them. The KJV follows the longer text in places, so 34 verse numbers have no line in Vaticanus (1:5, 1:7, 1:21 and others). The Plain gives each of them in square brackets, translated from a witness that has it, with a note saying which.

The Syriac. The Syriac Bible's Sirach was made from the Hebrew, though it was later revised by the Greek (Gigot).

The Latin. The Latin Bible's Sirach is an Old Latin version made before Jerome, from the Greek. Jerome translated other books afresh from the Hebrew, but this one he "revised but little" before it entered the Vulgate (Gigot). It has many additions, among them words of Wisdom about herself in chapter 24: where the Greek of 24:3 has her say "I came out of the Most High's mouth," the Latin that Cyprian quotes adds "first-born before every creature." The Douay-Rheims translates this Latin, so Catholic readers of older English Bibles meet a longer book than the Greek.

In the Greek manuscripts of Sirach two long passages stand in the reverse order from the Hebrew and the Latin. The Hebrew order is the natural one: the prayer for Israel (KJV 36:1–17) runs on without a break, and Ben Sira's words "I too kept watch, the last of all" and "Like a gleaner behind the grape pickers" stand together in one verse (KJV 33:16). In the Greek, the prayer is cut in two and its halves stand at 33:1–13 and 36:16–22, and the gleaner's line is split between 36:16 and 30:25. Gigot (1909) judged that the surviving Greek manuscripts all seem to come from a single Greek copy, which would explain why every one of them shares the same displacement. The displacement is easiest to explain if, in that copy, two groups of pages had been switched, while the Hebrew and the Latin, not copied from it, kept the order Ben Sira wrote.

The KJV and most English Bibles follow the Hebrew and Latin order, and so does Joseph Ziegler's Göttingen edition of the Greek, which, in the words of the NETS introduction, "has placed the Greek in the correct order"; the NRSV and NETS follow Ziegler, and NETS gives the manuscripts' numbers in parentheses. Swete's edition keeps the order of the Greek manuscripts. Other Bibles and editions may number these chapters differently, so check the numbers before citing. This site keeps the Greek order and Swete's numbers, because it translates the Greek, and every reference to Sirach on this site uses them. The text pages show the KJV under each Greek verse with its own number. In the tables, KJV numbers are written "KJV" and are not links: they are not this site's verses.

Sirach is not in the Jewish Bible, and the rabbis said so plainly. The Tosefta (Yadayim 2:13, which Sefaria numbers as paragraph 5 of chapter 2) rules: "The books of Ben Sira and all the books written from then on do not defile the hands." Books that "defile the hands" were the holy books, handled with special care; to say that a book does not defile the hands is to say that it is not Scripture. The phrase "from then on" suggests that the rabbis drew the line of Scripture before Ben Sira's time.

The Mishnah says that Rabbi Akiva counted among those who have no share in the world to come "one who reads external literature" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1, in the William Davidson translation). The Jerusalem Talmud gives as examples "the books of Ben Sirach and Ben Laana," while the books of Homer may be read "like a letter" (Sanhedrin 10:1). In the Babylonian Talmud Rav Yosef says that it is forbidden to read the book of Ben Sira. Abaye asks why, and runs through sayings that might be the reason: one on cooking fish, one on a father's sleepless worry for his daughter, one on keeping many people out of your house, and some odd proverbs about beards. For each but the last he shows the same thought in the Bible or in the sages. Rav Yosef answers that the excellent sayings in the book may still be taught, and quotes several, on the good wife and the bad (Sanhedrin 100b; compare Yevamot 63b).

So the book was kept out of the canon but not out of use. The Talmud quotes it "as it is written in the book of Ben Sira" on not searching out hidden things (Hagigah 13a, from 3:21–22), on a leader who frequents drinking houses (Niddah 16b), and on the son-in-law who lives in his father-in-law's house and the guest who brings in a guest (Bava Batra 98b). Once it even cites a saying about birds keeping company with their own kind as "triplicated in the Writings," the third part of the Bible, and attributes it to Ben Sira (Bava Kamma 92b; compare 13:15–16 and 27:9). In the Jerusalem Talmud Shimon ben Shetach quotes "the book of Ben Sirach" to King Yannai (Berakhot 7:2; compare 11:1). The Hebrew copies from Masada and Qumran, and the medieval copies found in Cairo, show Jews reading the book from the first century BC into the Middle Ages.

The Greek manuscripts and Fathers usually call the book "Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach" or simply "Wisdom of Sirach" (Gigot). The Latin church called it Ecclesiasticus, from as early as Cyprian of Carthage in the 200s, who quotes it "in Solomon, in Ecclesiasticus" (Testimonies 3.35, 3.51). The name means "of the church." Rufinus (about 404) explained that the Latins gave it this general title "designating not the author of the book, but the character of the writing": it was one of the "ecclesiastical" books read in the churches. Gigot calls it the church reading book. Luther's preface says the Latin title had been put into German as "die geistliche Zucht," spiritual discipline. It must not be confused with Ecclesiastes, which is Qohelet, one of the 66 books.

Christians used Sirach from early on as a book of moral teaching and of prophecy. Cyprian quotes it on good works and almsgiving (Testimonies 3.1) and reads Wisdom's words in chapter 24, in the Latin's longer form ("first-born before every creature"), as spoken of Christ, the Wisdom of God (2.1). Augustine found in it a prophecy of the faith of the nations, in the prayer "Have mercy upon us, O God, Ruler of all, and send Your fear upon all the nations" (here 33:1–3), and saw it "fulfilled through Jesus Christ" (City of God 17.20).

The Catholic lectionary reads it on Sundays and feasts: honor for father and mother on the feast of the Holy Family (3:2–6, 12–14); Wisdom's tent in Jacob on the Second Sunday after Christmas (24:1–2, 8–12); the free choice between fire and water (15:15–20); forgiving your neighbor so that your own sins are forgiven (27:30–28:7); humility (from chapter 3); the prayer of the lowly that "pierces the clouds" (from chapter 32 in this site's numbering, numbered 35 in the lectionary). Luther, for all his doubts about its rank, praised it as a book of household discipline and "a useful book for the common man" (our translation of "ein nützlich Buch fur den gemeinen Man").

Whether Christians should count it as Scripture is a question the churches answer differently. The answers are set side by side on the opening page of Proverbs, in the card that asks whether the Wisdom of Solomon and Sirach are part of Scripture.

Wisdom is the fear of the Lord and the keeping of the law. "All wisdom comes from the Lord" (1:1). The fear of the Lord is her beginning, fullness, crown and root (1:14–20). In chapter 24 Wisdom, who came from the mouth of the Most High, looks through all creation for a place to rest and is told to pitch her tent in Jacob; then the teacher says that all this is the book of the covenant, the law of Moses (24:23).

People choose. "Do not say, 'The Lord is the reason I turned away'" (15:11): God made the human being and "left him in the hand of his own choice" (15:14). Fire and water, life and death are set before each person, as in Deuteronomy 30:19.

Mercy to the poor counts with God. "Sins are atoned for by alms" (3:30), and the prayer of the humble and the widow reaches God (32:17–22). "Forgive the wrong your neighbor did to you, and then, when you pray, your own sins will be released" (28:2).

Death is the end of this life. Ben Sira looks for a good name and a blessed memory, not for resurrection: "In Hades, who will praise the Most High instead of the living, who give him thanks?" (17:27), and "in Hades no one argues over the length of a life" (41:4). Only the end of the Elijah passage may hint at more: "For we too will indeed live" (48:11), and what that means is debated.

Israel's story ends at the altar. The Hymn of the Fathers gives more lines to Aaron than to Moses, praises the covenant of priesthood with Phinehas, and closes with Simon the high priest coming out from the sanctuary in glory (45:6–26; 50:1–21).

spec.title: Why the Hymn of the Fathers skips Ezra
spec.body: This is Claude's theory. Ben Sira's survey ends with three men of the return: Zerubbabel and Jeshua son of Jozadak, who "built the house," and Nehemiah, who "lifted our fallen walls back up" and set up gates and bars (49:11–13). Then he turns to Simon, who repaired the house, strengthened the temple, dug the reservoir and fortified the city (50:1–4). Every man in that last stretch is a builder of the temple or the city. Ezra, the priest and scribe, built nothing; his work was the law. A scribe might be expected to praise him above all, and his absence has puzzled readers. The pattern suggests an answer: the final line of the hymn is chosen to lead from the builders of the return to Simon, the builder of Ben Sira's own day, and Ezra does not fit that line. Ben Sira gives the scribe's ideal elsewhere, in his own voice (38:24–39:11).

canon.summary: Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) is in the Old Testament of the Catholic Church and of the Orthodox churches, including the Ethiopian; Catholics call it deuterocanonical, and some Orthodox teachers rank it among the books "to be read." Anglicans and Lutherans place it among the Apocrypha, read for example of life but not to establish doctrine; Reformed, Baptist and most other Protestant churches do not count it as Scripture, and it is not in the Jewish Bible, though the rabbis quoted it.
accepted_by: Scripture, one of the deuterocanonical books. The Council of Carthage (397) counted "five books of Solomon," which in Augustine's usage included Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, and Augustine wrote that "of old the Church, especially the Western, received them into authority" (City of God 17.20). The Council of Trent (Session 4, 8 April 1546) named "Ecclesiasticus" among the sacred and canonical books, "entire with all their parts," as read in the Catholic Church and contained in the old Latin Vulgate, with an anathema on anyone who does not receive them. The Catechism (120) lists "Sirach (Ecclesiasticus)." The lectionary reads it on the feast of the Holy Family, on the Second Sunday after Christmas and on several Sundays of the year.

In the Old Testament, read in the Greek of the Septuagint. The Synod of Jerusalem (1672), answering the confession of Cyril Lucaris, named "the Wisdom of Sirach" with the Wisdom of Solomon, Judith, Tobit, the Maccabees and the additions to Daniel as "genuine parts of Scripture," while granting that not all of them had always been counted on the same level. Athanasius (367) had placed "the Wisdom of Sirach" among books not in the canon but "appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us," and Philaret's Russian catechism (questions 34–35) leaves "the Wisdom of the son of Sirach" out of its count of the Old Testament "because they do not exist in the Hebrew," citing Athanasius on how such books are to be read.
Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches
Scripture, in their 81-book Bible. The church's own list of its 46 Old Testament books has as number 45 the "Book of Joshua the son of Sirac."

Among the Apocrypha. Article VI of the Thirty-Nine Articles lists "Jesus the Son of Sirach" among "the other Books (as Hierome saith)" that "the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine." The King James Version (1611) printed it among the Apocrypha.

Among the Apocrypha. Luther's preface says the book "is not counted by the old fathers in the number of the Holy Scriptures, but held as a good, fine book of a wise man" (our translation of "von den alten Vetern nicht in der zal der heiligen Schrifft, sondern als sonst ein gut, fein Buch eins weisen Mans gehalten"), calls it a book of household discipline, "of the virtues of a godly master of a house," and "a useful book for the common man" (our translation of "ein nützlich Buch fur den gemeinen Man").

Not Scripture. The Belgic Confession (1561, article 6) lists "Jesus Sirach" among the apocryphal books the church may read and learn from "as far as they agree with the canonical books," but not to confirm "any point of faith or of the Christian religion." The Westminster Confession (1646, 1.3) says the Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon of the Scripture," to be used only like "other human writings."
Not Scripture. The Second London Baptist Confession (1689, 1.3) calls the Apocrypha "no part of the canon or rule of the Scripture."

Not Scripture. The Tosefta says that "the books of Ben Sira and all the books written from then on do not defile the hands" (Yadayim 2:13), and in the Talmud Rav Yosef forbids reading it, though he allows its good sayings to be taught (Sanhedrin 100b). Yet the rabbis quoted it often, once even as "in the Writings" (Bava Kamma 92b), and Jews copied its Hebrew into the Middle Ages.

Widely read and quoted, with different views of its rank. Cyprian (200s) quotes it often as "Ecclesiasticus" and "Solomon." Writers who followed the Hebrew count placed it lower: Athanasius among the books "to be read," Rufinus (about 404) among the "ecclesiastical" books read in the churches "but not appealed to for the confirmation of doctrine," and Jerome, who had seen it in Hebrew, among books read "for the strengthening of the people" but "not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas." Augustine and the African councils received it.

provenance.h: Who wrote it, where and when
provenance.b: A Jerusalem scribe and teacher, Jesus son of Eleazar son of Sirach (50:27), wrote it in Hebrew, about 180 BC (Rendsburg and Binstein; Gigot gives between 190 and 170 BC). He praises the high priest Simon son of Onias as a man of the recent past (50:1–21), and says nothing of the persecution under Antiochus, which Toy and Lévi date to 168 BC. His book draws on Proverbs and the other wisdom books, and on the law and the prophets, which he had studied all his life (the prologue).

His grandson came to Egypt in 132 BC, the thirty-eighth year of Ptolemy VIII Euergetes, and translated the book into Greek for the Jews there, adding the prologue. The Greek translation entered the Greek Bible of the Jews of Egypt, which the early church received. The Greek manuscripts usually give it the title "Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach" or "Wisdom of Sirach" (Gigot), and from the Greek it passed into the Latin, the Ethiopic and other Bibles; the Syriac was made from the Hebrew (Gigot).

Jews kept reading the Hebrew. A scroll of it copied in the first century BC was left at Masada, pieces of it were at Qumran, the rabbis quoted it, Jerome saw a copy, and Jews were still copying it in the Middle Ages. Those medieval copies were put away in the Genizah of a Cairo synagogue and came to light from 1896 on. About two-thirds of the Hebrew is known today (see "The Hebrew, lost and found").

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: Judaism's Bible does not contain it, and the rabbis said why in their own terms: the books of Ben Sira "and all the books written from then on" do not defile the hands (Tosefta Yadayim 2:13). The words "from then on" suggest that the rabbis drew the line of Scripture before Ben Sira's time. Protestants put the argument in its strongest form: the oracles of God were entrusted to Israel (Romans 3:2); Jesus spoke of the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms (Luke 24:44), the three parts the grandson's prologue already names; and, they add, no New Testament writer quotes Sirach by name or as Scripture. So the church should receive the books Israel received. Philaret's Orthodox catechism uses the same reason, "they do not exist in the Hebrew," to leave it out of the count, though the Hebrew original has since been found in part.

Jerome knew the Hebrew of Sirach, "titled not Ecclesiasticus as among the Latins, but Parables," and still ranked it below the canonical books: as the church reads Judith, Tobit and the Maccabees without receiving them among the canonical Scriptures, so it may read Wisdom and Sirach "for the strengthening of the people, (but) not for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical dogmas." Athanasius (367) set "the Wisdom of Sirach" among the books "to be read" by those preparing to join the church, and Rufinus (about 404) among the "ecclesiastical" books. These are the roots of Article VI, which quotes Jerome by name.

Luther's preface says the old fathers did not count it among the Holy Scriptures but held it as the good book of a wise man, a collection "from many books" with no strict order, and he valued it for teaching households. The Belgic Confession and the Westminster Confession went further: such books may be read, but no point of faith may rest on them. Readers who weigh the book against the 66 point to passages that sit uneasily beside them: almsgiving that atones for sins (3:30), a line that lays the beginning of sin and death on a woman (25:24), harsh words about daughters (42:9–14), and no clear hope of life after death (17:27; 41:4). The chapter pages give the readings, and the Tobit card on almsgiving (Tobit 4) and the free-will card on chapter 15 set out how the churches answer.

rejected_why.h: How the churches that keep it answer
rejected_why.b: Catholic and Orthodox teachers answer that the church received the Old Testament in Greek, the Bible of the apostles' Greek-speaking churches, and read Sirach in public from the early centuries, so much that the Latins called it the church book. Augustine pointed out that the Western church had long received it into authority even though it was not Solomon's, and the African councils counted it among the books of Solomon. Catholics add that the canon was the church's to recognize, as Carthage and Trent did, and the Synod of Jerusalem answered that books not always counted on the same level had been reckoned with Scripture by synods and ancient theologians. On the hard verses they read Sirach as Proverbs is read, as wisdom that must be taken with the whole of Scripture. Whether it is Scripture is set out side by side on the opening page of Proverbs.

cited_in.b: Jesus says, "Come to me, all of you who are worn out and loaded down, and I myself will give you rest" and "Lift my yoke onto yourselves ... And you will find rest for your souls" (Matthew 11:28–29). Ben Sira's closing poem calls the untaught to draw near to him (Ἐγγίσατε πρὸς μέ, 51:23), to put their necks under the yoke (ζυγόν, 51:26), and says that with a little labor he found much rest (ἀνάπαυσιν, 51:27); chapter 6 speaks of Wisdom's yoke and the rest she gives in the end (6:24–30). The words "to me," "yoke" and "rest" are shared, and in both a teacher of wisdom calls the weary. The difference matters as much: Ben Sira invites pupils to Wisdom, Jesus invites them to himself, so Jesus can be read as speaking as Wisdom in person; or both may draw on a common Jewish way of speaking about the yoke of wisdom and of the law, without Matthew depending on Sirach.

In Jesus' parable the rich fool says to himself, "Soul, you have lots of good things stored up, enough for many years. Rest now. Eat, drink, celebrate," and God says, "Fool! On this very night they demand your soul back from you" (Luke 12:19–20). Ben Sira describes a man grown rich by care and thrift who says, "I have found rest, and now I will feast on my good things," while "he does not know how much time will go by before he leaves them to others and dies" (11:19). The story, the rest, the eating and the good things (ἀνάπαυσιν ... φάγομαι ἐκ τῶν ἀγαθῶν μου; Luke ἀναπαύου, φάγε) are close. The likeness is close, though the warning about a rich man's sudden death is also found elsewhere (Psalm 49; Ecclesiastes 2:18–21).

Jesus' parable of the widow and the unjust judge ends, "Will God, then, not get justice for his chosen, who call out to him day and night? Is he slow to act for them? I tell you, he will give them justice without delay" (Luke 18:7–8). Ben Sira says that the Lord is a judge who shows no favoritism, does not ignore the widow when she pours out her complaint, and that the prayer of the humble pierces the clouds; "the Lord will not delay, nor will he be patient with them, until he has broken the backs of the merciless" (32:22). Luke's Greek "is he slow to act for them" (μακροθυμεῖ ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς) has the same verb and preposition as Sirach's (μακροθυμήσει ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς, 32:22), Luke in the present tense and Sirach in the future. The widow, the judge, the delay and that phrase together make a case that Luke's parable echoes this passage (numbered as chapter 35 in most English Bibles), though the widow crying to God is an old theme of the law and the prophets (Exodus 22:22–23).

Jesus teaches, "forgive us the debts we owe, just as we ourselves have forgiven the people who owe us," and "If you forgive people their wrongs, you too will be forgiven by your heavenly Father" (Matthew 6:12, 14). Ben Sira: "Forgive the wrong your neighbor did to you, and then, when you pray, your own sins will be released" (28:2; ἄφες ἀδίκημα ... αἱ ἁμαρτίαι σου λυθήσονται); a man who keeps anger against another cannot ask the Lord for healing (28:3–5). The thought is the same. Whether Jesus knew Sirach or both express a teaching common among Jews is not something the texts can settle; the words are different.

James writes, "let every person be ready to listen, slow to talk, slow to anger" (James 1:19); the Greek is "quick to hear" (ταχὺς εἰς τὸ ἀκοῦσαι). Ben Sira: "Be swift when it comes to listening, and give your reply with patience" (5:11), with the same word for quick (ταχύς). James is full of wisdom teaching like Sirach's, on the tongue, the rich and testing, and he may have known the book; but advice to listen before speaking is common (Proverbs 18:13), so this one parallel proves little by itself.

"And the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us" (John 1:14). In Sirach 24 Wisdom says that the Creator of all made her tent rest and told her, "Pitch your tent in Jacob" (24:8; Ἐν Ἰακὼβ κατασκήνωσον); she served before him in the holy tent and was set firm in Zion (24:10). John's verb is the same root (ἐσκήνωσεν). Both texts say that what was with God from the beginning came to dwell among God's people, and John's prologue as a whole can be read against the Jewish picture of Wisdom. The shared root is real, but nothing shows that John drew on Sirach 24 rather than on that wider picture. The difference is the heart of John's claim: for Ben Sira, Wisdom's dwelling is the law of Moses (24:23); for John, it is a man.

The angel says John will go ahead of the Lord "with Elijah's spirit and power. He will turn fathers' hearts back to their children" (Luke 1:17). Ben Sira says of Elijah, "You were written down in warnings for the times to come, to still anger before it turns to rage, to turn the heart of the father back to the son, and to set the tribes of Jacob on their feet" (48:10). Both take up Malachi 4:5–6 (Malachi 3:23–24 in the Hebrew); Sirach's Greek "heart of a father toward a son" (καρδίαν πατρὸς πρὸς υἱὸν) is word for word the Greek of Malachi, while Luke has the plurals, "hearts of fathers to children." After Malachi, Sirach shows Jews still expecting Elijah's return, and it adds a task from Isaiah 49:6, the restoring of the tribes. Luke depends on Malachi; the link with Sirach is a shared hope, not a quotation.

Hebrews: "By faith Enoch was carried off ... For before he was carried off, it was witnessed of him that he had pleased God" (Hebrews 11:5). Sirach: "Enoch pleased the Lord and was carried off, a pattern of repentance for the generations" (44:16; εὐηρέστησεν Κυρίῳ καὶ μετετέθη). Both use the Greek of Genesis 5:24, where "walked with God" became "pleased God" and "God took him" became "God carried him off." The likeness comes from the shared Greek Genesis. Each also adds its own lesson: Sirach repentance (the Hebrew has "a sign of knowledge"), Hebrews faith. Hebrews 11 as a whole is, like Sirach 44–50, a roll call of Israel's heroes, and the two lists invite comparison.

James asks whether Abraham was not "justified by works" when he offered Isaac (James 2:21). Sirach says Abraham kept the law of the Most High, entered a covenant with him, and "under testing he was found faithful" (44:20; ἐν πειρασμῷ εὑρέθη πιστός); 1 Maccabees 2:52 joins the same words to Genesis 15:6, as James does. All three stand in a Jewish tradition that read Genesis 22 as Abraham's great test. James need not depend on Sirach; he shares its way of reading Abraham, which Paul answers differently (Romans 4:2–3).

Luke's Gospel ends with Jesus lifting his hands and blessing his disciples (ἐπάρας τὰς χεῖρας αὐτοῦ εὐλόγησεν, Luke 24:50), and the disciples in the temple blessing God. Sirach 50:20–22 has Simon the high priest come down, lift his hands over the whole assembly of Israel to give the Lord's blessing, and the people bow a second time; then the call to bless God. The gesture is the priest's (Leviticus 9:22), so Luke may be drawing on the law, on the temple service as Sirach describes it, or on neither. The link is suggestive but cannot be proved.

In Mark's list of commandments Jesus adds one not among the Ten: "You must not cheat" (Μὴ ἀποστερήσῃς, Mark 10:19). Sirach 4:1 has the same verb in the same form: "My child, do not rob the poor man of what he lives on" (τὴν ζωὴν τοῦ πτωχοῦ μὴ ἀποστερήσῃς); the Plain renders it "rob" there and "cheat" in Mark. The same verb is used in the Greek of Exodus 21:10 and of Malachi 3:5 (those who cheat the hired worker of his wages), so Mark's word may come from the law or the prophets as easily as from Sirach. The link is possible, not proved.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Judaism before Jesus, Sirach is of great value: it is a book with a named author, a home in Jerusalem and a firm date, written by a scribe who knew the temple, the priests and the law from the inside, and it shows what a faithful Jew taught about wisdom, the law, the poor, prayer, death and Israel's history about 180 BC. As a text it survived unevenly: the Greek is complete but is a translation, displaced in chapters 30–36 and expanded in some copies, and the Hebrew original survives for about two-thirds of the book in medieval copies checked by older scrolls from Masada and Qumran. It makes few historical claims beyond its own date and its retelling of the Bible's story. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees with Proverbs, Deuteronomy and the Psalms on nearly every point of conduct and faith; it goes beyond them in joining Wisdom to the law and in teaching that almsgiving atones; and it stands in tension with later Scripture in having no clear hope of resurrection and in a few harsh lines about women.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Judaism before Jesus: very high
sections.b: The book can be dated and placed well. The prologue fixes the translation in Egypt after 132 BC, the praise of Simon son of Onias (50:1–21) places the author in Jerusalem in the generation before the Maccabean revolt, and the book shows a world on the eve of that crisis: a city proud of its temple and priests, scribes who served the rich and the powerful, Greek ways pressing in. It shows which books Ben Sira knew (the law, the prophets, "the other books") and how he read them. The Hymn of the Fathers retells Israel's story from Enoch to Nehemiah, and its "bones of the Twelve Prophets" (49:10) treat the minor prophets as one group. The New Testament's talk of Wisdom, of forgiving to be forgiven, of the yoke and the rest, is easier to understand with Sirach in hand.

sections.h: 2. The text: complicated, and much better known than a century ago
sections.b: The churches received the grandson's Greek, which is complete, in the codices of the 300s and 400s. But all known Greek manuscripts share the displacement of chapters 30–36, some add lines (the longer text), and the Latin adds more. The Hebrew original was lost to Christian readers until 1896. The Genizah leaves are medieval, and they differ from each other; the Masada scroll, copied in the first century BC, overlaps with the medieval manuscript B in chapters 39–44 (Rendsburg and Binstein), so the two can be compared directly, and the NETS translator judges that the Hebrew manuscripts preserve Ben Sira's Hebrew "in their essentials." So the meaning of most verses is secure, but many single words and lines are uncertain, and the Plain's variant notes give the Hebrew wherever it differs in meaning.

sections.h: 3. Its claims about itself and history
sections.b: The book claims only what can be checked: a named author in Jerusalem, a grandson in Egypt, a high priest of the recent past. These fit what is known of the time: the Oniad family held the high priesthood in Jerusalem in those years (see the topic page on Onias). Its retelling of the Bible's story in chapters 44–49 follows the books of the Bible closely, with Ben Sira's own judgments: Enoch carried off as an example (44:16; 49:14), Samuel prophesying after his death (46:20, as in 1 Samuel 28), Elijah to return before the day of the LORD (48:10, from Malachi). Where it adds details, as of Simon's temple service (50:5–21), it is an eyewitness of its own day.

Where it agrees. The fear of the Lord as the beginning of wisdom (1:14; Proverbs 1:7); one God, Creator and judge, merciful and forgiving (2:11; Exodus 34:6); honor for parents (3:1–16); care for the poor, the orphan and the widow (4:1–10; 32:17–22); human responsibility before God (15:11–20; Deuteronomy 30:19); the dangers of the tongue, wealth and pride; Israel's story as God's faithfulness.

Where it goes beyond. It identifies Wisdom with the law of Moses (24:23). It says almsgiving atones for sins (3:30), close to Daniel 4:27 and Proverbs 16:6, and like Tobit 12:9. Catholic and Orthodox readers see here a true teaching on mercy and repentance; Protestants read it as works joined to grace in a way Paul would not, or as poetry about mercy that should not be pressed (see the almsgiving card at Tobit 4). It praises the doctor and his medicines as God's gift (38:1–15), a theme the Bible touches only in passing.

Where it stands in tension. Ben Sira has no clear hope of life after death: "In Hades, who will praise the Most High instead of the living, who give him thanks?" (17:27; compare Psalm 6:5), and death is "the Lord's sentence on all flesh" (41:4). Daniel 12:2 and the New Testament go further; Christians who hold the book as Scripture read this as the Old Testament's stage before the full revelation, as they read Psalm 6. His line "The beginning of sin is from a woman, and on account of her we all die" (25:24) stands beside Genesis 3, where both the woman and the man eat, and Romans 5:12, which lays sin's entry on "one man"; readers differ on whether he means Eve or the bad wife of 25:16–26 (see the note there). His words on daughters and women (22:3; 42:9–14) reflect his time and his audience of young men, and the rabbis already argued over them (Sanhedrin 100b). The free-will card on chapter 15 shows how the churches read his teaching on choice.

how_to_read.b: If you are Catholic or Orthodox, Sirach is in your Old Testament; Catholics hear it on the feast of the Holy Family and on Sundays. If you are Protestant, it is not Scripture for you, but Luther called it a useful book for every household and the Anglican tradition reads it for example of life. For everyone it is a window into the faith of Jerusalem about 180 BC.

how_to_read.h: Read it as a teacher's lessons
how_to_read.b: Take a chapter at a time, as a student would have heard it. Most sayings are practical and meant for young men of the time: how to behave at a rich man's table, how to lend, how to choose a friend. Ask what each one was meant to teach those first hearers before asking what it means now.

how_to_read.h: Read it beside Proverbs and the Bible's history
how_to_read.b: Read Proverbs 1–9 before Sirach 1–6, Proverbs 8 beside Sirach 24, and Genesis to Nehemiah beside the Hymn of the Fathers (44–49): see whom Ben Sira praises, what he says about each, and whom he leaves out. Then read Matthew 11:25–30, Luke 12:16–21 and Luke 18:1–8, and judge for yourself how close Jesus' words come.

how_to_read.h: Mind the numbers and the two texts
how_to_read.b: When you look up Sirach in another Bible, check chapters 30–36: this site uses the Greek numbers, and most English Bibles use the Hebrew and Latin order (see the table). Remember too that this is a translation of a translation: where the Hebrew survives, the variant notes say what Ben Sira himself wrote.

how_to_read.h: Using it in study or teaching
how_to_read.b: When you quote it, say what it is: "Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), in the Old Testament of Catholic and Orthodox Christians and among the Apocrypha for Protestants," and give the numbering you use. It is good background for the New Testament's teaching on Wisdom, on forgiving and being forgiven, and on prayer and the poor.
